A path-traversal-safe static file handler over `http`. Resolves an attacker-controlled request
path to a file under a configured root directory and streams it as an HTTP response, with correct
caching, conditional-request and byte-range semantics. Usage: see ./README.md.

The two make-or-break invariants:

1. **Containment.** A served file is *always* inside the configured root. No request — under any
   percent-encoding, path separator, `..` sequence, NUL byte or symlink — ever reads a byte
   outside it.
2. **No panics.** Every failure maps to an HTTP status (301/400/403/404/405/414/416/500); only a
   genuine response-write failure propagates (so the server can close the connection).

## 1. Path-traversal threat model

The request path (`req.path`) is untrusted. The defense is **two independent layers**, both
required — string sanitization alone is necessary but not sufficient (a symlink defeats it), and
`openat`-relative opening alone would still let a decoded `..` or an absolute path through.

### Layer 1 — `sanitizePath` (string)

Percent-decode `req.path`, then, on the **decoded** bytes:

| Vector | Handling |
|---|---|
| `..` segment (`/../`, `..%2f`, `%2e%2e/`, doubly-encoded) | **rejected** — `error.Traversal`. Decode happens first, so every encoding of `..` collapses to the same literal segment before the check. |
| NUL byte (`%00` or literal `\x00`) | **rejected** — `error.InvalidByte` (defeats C-string path truncation). |
| Backslash (`\` or `%5c`) | **rejected** — `error.InvalidByte` (a Windows path separator; refused cross-platform). |
| Absolute path (`/etc/passwd`) | **neutralized** — the leading `/` is stripped and the result is root-relative; there is no way to express an absolute filesystem path. |
| Dotfile segment (`.git`, `.env`) | **rejected by default** — `error.DotfileForbidden` (opt-in via `serve_dotfiles`). |
| `.` and empty (`//`) segments | **collapsed** (dropped). |
| Malformed `%`-encoding | **rejected** — `error.Malformed`. |
| Decoded path > `max_path_bytes` (8 KiB) | **rejected** — `error.TooLong`. |

The output is a clean path with single `/` separators, no leading/trailing slash, and no
`.`/`..`/empty segments. An empty result means the request targets the root directory itself.
Compaction is in-place and allocation-free.

A **trailing slash** says the request names a DIRECTORY (`namesDirectory`: the decoded path ends
in `/`, ignoring trailing `.` segments — `/a.txt/`, `/a.txt%2f`, `/a.txt/.`). Layer 1 drops that
slash, so the serve paths (`Handler.serve`, `resolveFile`, `Snapshot`/`Live`) carry the fact
separately and open the leaf as a directory only: a regular file there is **404** (POSIX
`ENOTDIR`, nginx, Apache), never the file. Serving `/secret.txt/` as `/secret.txt` would let one
added character bypass an exact-path rule in a proxy in front (found by the Go `net/http` oracle,
Anchoring).

Note: `%2f` decodes to a real `/` — after decoding it is a genuine segment separator, not a
traversal (a nested path like `a%2fb.txt` becomes `a/b.txt`). Because every `..` is rejected
regardless of encoding, an encoded slash can never help an escape.

### Layer 2 — `openWithinRoot` (filesystem)

The sanitized path is opened **one component at a time, each relative to the previous directory
handle** (`std.Io.Dir.openDir` / `openFile`): a single slash-free segment is all the OS resolver
ever sees, so a decoded `..` — even if layer 1 somehow missed one — cannot combine across
components. `follow_symlinks = false` (the default) passes `O_NOFOLLOW`, so a symlinked component
is an open error rather than a traversal. `resolve_beneath = true` is additionally requested
(`openat2(RESOLVE_BENEATH)` / `O_BENEATH` where supported; ignored elsewhere) as defense-in-depth.

Given: (a) no `..` segment survives layer 1, (b) each component is opened relative to a handle
rooted at the configured root, and (c) no symlink is traversed — the opened file is **provably**
within the root.

### Symlink policy

- **Default (`follow_symlinks = false`):** symlinks are never traversed. A symlinked path
  component yields an open error → **403**. A symlink inside the root pointing anywhere outside it
  is therefore unreachable. This is the hard, portable guarantee and the mode the test suite
  exercises against a real out-of-root file.
- **Opt-in (`follow_symlinks = true`):** symlinks are followed, but after opening, the file's real
  path (`realPath`) is verified to be a path-separated prefix match under the root's real path
  (`verifyContained`); an escaping symlink is still refused (**403**). If the OS cannot produce a
  real path, the file is treated as uncontained and refused (fail-closed).

### Non-regular files

A FIFO, device or socket is never opened (`openServable`): the leaf, an index and a precompressed
sibling are `stat`ed first and anything but a regular file or directory is 403. Opening a FIFO with
no writer blocks in `open(2)` forever, so one request per FIFO in the root would pin a connection
thread — an `fstat` check after the open never runs. std 0.17 has no
`O_NONBLOCK` open on Linux, hence the stat; a FIFO swapped in between stat and open needs write
access to the root. `Snapshot`/`Live` only ever open entries the walk saw as regular files. A
directory named like a variant (`app.js.br/`) is not one.

### Dotfile policy

Segments beginning with `.` are refused by default (so `.git`, `.env`, `.htaccess` are never
served) at layer 1, and the directory listing likewise skips them. `serve_dotfiles = true` allows
them everywhere.

### Tested vectors

`../../etc/passwd`, `..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd`, `%2e%2e/…`, `....//…` (refused as a dotfile),
absolute `/etc/passwd`, `foo%00.png`, `..\..\…`, a symlink inside the root pointing to an
out-of-root secret, and `sub/../../secret.txt` — each must be a 4xx and must never return the
out-of-root content. Positive controls (`/hello.txt`, `/sub/dir/file.txt`, `/` → index) are served
alongside. See the module tests (`std.testing.tmpDir` builds the root, a real out-of-root secret,
and the escaping symlink).

## 2. Response semantics

### MIME

`Content-Type` by file extension: `Options.mime_overrides` first (case-insensitive), then the
embedded table (html, htm, css, js, mjs, json, map, xml, txt, md, csv, svg, png, apng, jpg, jpeg,
gif, webp, avif, heic, tif, tiff, ico, bmp, woff, woff2, ttf, otf, eot, wasm, pdf, zip, gz, zst, tar,
epub, webmanifest, jsonld, xhtml, rss, atom, ics, wav, mp3, aac, flac, m4a, weba, ogg, oga, opus,
mp4, mov, webm, ogv, avi, mpeg, mpg, glb, gltf — the common web types of nginx's `mime.types`),
then `Options.default_mime` (`application/octet-stream`). No dot / unknown extension → default.
There is no content sniffing (Go sniffs the first 512 bytes of an unknown extension): a body whose
type the extension does not name is served as the default, and `nosniff` (below) tells the browser
not to guess either. Text types carry `charset=utf-8`; binary ones do not.

Every representation response (200/206, not 304/412/416) also carries `X-Content-Type-Options:
nosniff` (best-effort — losing it on header-budget exhaustion does not escalate to 500, unlike
`Content-Type` itself). `Content-Type` from the table above is already the primary defense against
MIME-sniffing; `nosniff` is defense in depth against a browser second-guessing it anyway. The
module does not offer `Content-Disposition: attachment` or any other way to force a download — an
uploaded `.html`/`.svg` inside the root is still served as an executable document on the serving
origin if the caller allows such uploads into the root at all (A1 F18; this is the same trade-off
Go's `net/http` `FileServer` and nginx make, not a gap specific to this module).

### Validators

- **`Last-Modified`**: the file's mtime (`stat.mtime`), formatted as an IMF-fixdate. As an `If-Range` date it
  counts only when strong (at least one second before the response's `Date`, RFC 9110 §8.8.2.2); a file
  modified within the last second answers a date-conditioned `Range` with the full 200.
- **`ETag`**: `"<size:hex>-<mtime_seconds:hex>"`, **weak** (`W/` prefix) by default (A1 F5) —
  `Options.strong_etag = true` selects the strong form. Weak
  is the safe choice: `mtime`'s granularity is one SECOND, so a same-second, same-size edit (an
  atomic `rename` over a file of identical length) leaves a STRONG tag unchanged despite RFC 9110
  §8.8.1 requiring a strong validator to change on every representation edit — and a strong tag
  authorizes `If-Range` to splice bytes from two file versions into one response (RFC 9110
  §13.1.5). A weak tag cannot authorize `If-Range` at all, closing the splice outright; the cost is
  that byte-range RESUME never succeeds for any client, since a weak validator can never authorize
  a range response either. `Options.strong_etag` exists for an operator who needs resume and either
  accepts that gap or does not do same-size same-second in-place edits. Computing the tag is cheap
  either way — no file read — and it changes on any edit that moves the size or mtime. A content
  hash is strong against same-second, same-size touches too, at the cost of reading the file:
  `Handler` does not offer it (see *What is deliberately not done*), the `Snapshot`/`Live` content
  tags do (§3.7).

Both computed header values live in plain locals, not threadlocal scratch: the response writer's
`setHeader` copies the bytes into its own storage at call time (`http`'s `putHeader` → `dupe`), so
the locals only need to outlive the `setHeader` calls that pass them, not the response (see
`root.zig`'s own "Locals, not thread-locals" comment at the `sendFile` call site). Nothing here is
a threadlocal buffer the writer borrows.

### Conditional requests (RFC 9110 §8.8/§13)

Delegated to `http.conditional.apply`, evaluated **before** range handling so a 304/412
short-circuits early. `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` (GET/HEAD) → **304 Not Modified** (no
body); `If-Match` / `If-Unmodified-Since` → **412 Precondition Failed**. A 304 carries `ETag`,
`Last-Modified` and `Cache-Control` (representation-specific headers are set only on the
proceeding 200/206 path).

### Range requests (RFC 7233)

Delegated to `http.range.apply`. `Accept-Ranges: bytes` is always set.

| Request | Response |
|---|---|
| No (or malformed) `Range` | **200**, `Content-Length: <size>`, full body. |
| Single satisfiable range | **206**, `Content-Range: bytes s-e/total`, `Content-Length: <range len>`, the range bytes (streamed positionally). |
| Unsatisfiable range | **416**, `Content-Range: bytes */total`, empty body. |
| Multiple ranges | **200**, full body (multi-range served as a whole; RFC 7233 §6.1 permits ignoring `Range`). |

Body bytes are streamed positionally in 64 KiB chunks (`readPositionalAll`) — the whole file is
never buffered, so large files cost bounded memory. A `HEAD` sets the same framing headers and
writes no body.

### Directory handling

A URL naming a directory but missing its trailing slash is redirected **301** to the
slash-terminated form first (`Options.redirect_to_trailing_slash`, default true — A1 F17,
round-2 Q8), matching Go `net/http` `FileServer` / nginx: `GET /sub` → `301 Location: /sub/`, query
string preserved. The `Location` starts with exactly one `/`: `//docs` names the directory `docs`
(empty segments are dropped), and a `Location: //docs/` would be a protocol-relative URL to the host
`docs`, an open redirect (Go answers with relative Locations, nginx merges slashes). Without this, `/sub` and `/sub/` silently served the identical content under two
different URLs, and a relative link/asset inside that page resolves against whichever one the
browser's address bar shows — correct only from the slash-terminated form. Set
`redirect_to_trailing_slash = false` to serve both forms. A plain file is never
redirected regardless of its name.

Past that redirect, a directory request resolves to `Options.index` (`index.html`). With no index:
**403** by default, or an HTML listing when `directory_listing = true`. Each listing entry is a
relative link (`<a href>` percent-encoded down to the RFC 3986 unreserved bytes, text HTML-escaped
`& < > " '` so a crafted filename cannot inject markup, a `/` after a directory; as Go `FileServer`
and nginx `autoindex` do); dotfile entries are skipped unless `serve_dotfiles` is set. The listing
carries `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` (a failure to set it is a 500), the configured
`Cache-Control` (likewise a 500 when it cannot be set) and best-effort `nosniff`. An I/O error
before the first entry answers 500; one after it ends the list with a `[listing incomplete]` row (the
status is already sent), and `Options.max_listing_entries` (default 10 000, skipped dotfiles count)
ends it with a `[listing truncated]` row.

### Cache-Control

`Options.cache_control`, when set, is emitted verbatim on 200/206 responses (e.g.
`public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for fingerprinted assets).

## 3. Status mapping

| Condition | Status |
|---|---|
| Non-GET/HEAD method | 405 (+ `Allow: GET, HEAD`) |
| Directory URL missing its trailing slash (A1 F17, default on) | 301 (+ `Location`) |
| Traversal / dotfile / backslash-or-NUL / forbidden (symlink, non-regular file, escape) | 403 |
| Malformed percent-encoding | 400 |
| Decoded path too long | 414 |
| Missing file/directory, or a single path segment over the filesystem's `NAME_MAX` (A1 F13, round-2 Q5: no file of that name can exist, same fact as any other missing name) | 404 |
| Unsatisfiable range | 416 |
| Real I/O / filesystem failure | 500 |
| 304 / 412 | per conditional evaluation |

## 3.5. Serving an already-opened file

`Handler.sendFile(req, rw, *Opened)` is the internal second half of `serve` — everything after
`resolveFile` succeeds (validators, conditional evaluation, range handling, body) — made public. It
exists so a caller who resolved/opened the file itself (typically: `resolveFile` up front to
compose an app-specific 404 instead of `serve`'s built-in one) does not pay a second resolve. It
borrows `opened`; it never closes it, matching `serve`'s own `defer opened.close(h.io)` at its one
internal call site. Status-mapping for a *failed* resolve is entirely the caller's problem —
`sendFile` starts from an already-successful `Opened` and only covers what `serve` does from that
point on.

## 3.6. `Snapshot` — a root opened once

`Snapshot.open(gpa, io, root, opts)` walks `root` once (dotfiles skipped unless `serve_dotfiles`,
depth ≤ `max_depth`), opens every regular file through `openWithinRoot` — the same layer-2 walk a
request takes — and keeps the descriptors, their `stat` and a path table. `serve(io, req, rw,
raw_path)` then does `sanitizePath` (layer 1, unchanged), one table lookup, and `sendFile` through
the `Io` it is given: **no `openat`/`stat`/`getdents` after `open`.** For a process that sandboxes
path-based opens (Landlock re-checks every open, even relative to a directory fd opened before) or
an event loop whose file opens would block a shared thread.

Differences from `Handler`, all by construction: a symlink (any non-regular entry) is not in the
table — 404, where `Handler` answers 403; a directory whose index is a symlink is a directory
with no index (301 then 403, where `Handler` answers 403). No directory listing, no
`follow_symlinks`, no SPA `fallback` (each `error.Unsupported` at `open`, never ignored silently). A file created after `open` is a 404; one
replaced by rename keeps serving the old inode until the next snapshot. `max_files` bounds the
descriptors and `max_dirs` the directories (both `error.TooManyFiles`, never a partial table),
`max_depth` the nesting (`error.TooDeep`, as is a path longer than `max_path_bytes`, which no request could carry: refused rather than held unreachable, so a deep tree fails closed at `open`). `max_entries` (default 0 = unbounded, as nginx and Go) bounds the directory entries read of every kind, symlinks and sockets included (`error.TooManyFiles`). `TooDeep`/`TooManyFiles` abort the whole rescan, so one new deep directory keeps `Live` on the old generation (reported as `failed`): publishing a partial tree would trade the completeness guarantee for availability. The walk reads an entry's kind from the directory entry;
on a filesystem that reports DT_UNKNOWN (some XFS, NFS, FUSE) it classifies the entry with one
no-follow `fstatat` (`Snapshot.realKind`, as `find`/`ftw` do; the directory listing uses it too), a
failed stat skips the entry, and a symlink stays unserved. A test serves one fixture tree through
both and requires the same status, body, `Location` and `ETag` for every non-symlink path,
traversal vectors included.

**Precompressed variants.** `name.br`, `name.zst`, `name.gz` found next to `name` are its variants
(`SnapshotOptions.precompressed`, all on by default). A request for `name` gets one when
`Accept-Encoding` (via `http.conneg.negotiateEncoding`, ties → br, zstd, gzip) prefers it over
`identity` (`encodingQuality(…, "identity")`): the variant's bytes, `Content-Encoding`, `name`'s
`Content-Type`, the variant's own `ETag`/`Last-Modified` (so 304 and Range apply to the encoded
bytes, as nginx `gzip_static` does). No `Accept-Encoding` → identity. Every answer for a name that
has variants carries `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (not best-effort: without it a shared cache serves one
client's coding to another). Variants remain servable under their own names.

**`Handler` has the same, per request, opt-in** (`Options.precompressed: ?Precompressed = null`,
`.{}` = all three; `SnapshotOptions.precompressed` is still the `Snapshot`'s own and the option in
`SnapshotOptions.serve` is ignored there). The negotiation is the one function both use
(`pickCoding`: `negotiateEncoding` + the identity check). A request opens only the siblings it needs:
the best acceptable coding is tried with `openWithinRoot` (so a symlinked, escaping, non-regular or
missing sibling is simply not a variant), and when it is absent the next best is tried; no
`Accept-Encoding` opens nothing. Index files have variants too (`/sub/` → `sub/index.html.br`).
Answers: `Content-Encoding`, `Content-Type` from the ORIGINAL name, the variant's size/mtime for
`Last-Modified` and `Content-Length`, and an `ETag` that carries the coding's token
(`W/"<size>-<mtime>-br"`) so two encodings of one file never share a validator even at equal size
and mtime. Range, `If-Range` (with `strong_etag`) and 304 act on the encoded bytes, as nginx
`gzip_static` and Go do. Unlike the `Snapshot`, a `Handler` cannot know without probing whether a
file has siblings, so with the option on EVERY file answer carries `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, siblings
or not (cost: a cache keyed by encoding for files that have one coding only). The server core's own
compression stays off for these, because a handler-set `Content-Encoding` disables it.

**SPA fallback** (`Options.fallback: ?[]const u8 = null`, `Handler` only). A GET/HEAD whose path
resolves to nothing (the 404 case; a 403 or 400 is never rewritten), whose last decoded segment has
no `.` and whose `Accept` lists `text/html` with a non-zero weight (case-insensitive; `*/*` does not
count, `text/html;q=0` refuses) is answered with the fallback
file: 200, the file's `Content-Type`/`ETag`/`Last-Modified`, conditional and Range rules, its
precompressed variants when those are on. It is served at the requested URL (no trailing-slash
redirect), with `Vary: Accept` because the same URL is a 404 to another `Accept` — and that 404 carries
`Vary: Accept` too (a cached 404 for an API client must not be served to a later navigation). The fallback path
is resolved by the same `resolveForServe` as a request: sanitizing, no-follow walk, dotfile policy,
containment under `follow_symlinks`; a fallback that is missing, refused, a symlink under
no-follow, or a directory with no index leaves the ordinary 404 (a directory WITH an index serves
the index). An extension is any `.` in the last segment, so `/missing.js` and `/v1.2` stay 404s: a
broken asset link is never answered with HTML. Other methods keep 405. The multi-range
`multipart/byteranges` item stays refused.

## 3.7. Content tags, and `Live` — a snapshot that follows its directory

`SnapshotOptions.fingerprint` (default on): every file is hashed once when it enters a snapshot
(SHA-256), and its `ETag` is `"` + the first 128 bits in hex + `"` — a **strong** validator in the
full §8.8.1 sense, since it changes exactly when the bytes do, so `If-Range` may authorize a range
(resumed downloads work, unlike with the weak size+mtime tag) and a rewrite with identical bytes
keeps its tag. `Handler.sendFileTagged` takes the tag; `sendFile` is it with null. A file larger than
`SnapshotOptions.max_fingerprint_bytes` (64 MiB) keeps `Handler`'s size+mtime tag instead, so one
huge file cannot make `open` or a `Live` rescan read gigabytes; a file is hashed up to the size it
had when opened, never past it.

`Live` rescans (`reload`, or `start`'s thread every `rescan_ms`) and publishes a new generation when
anything changed. A generation is built from the previous one: a file whose `fstatat` (no follow)
shows the same inode, size and mtime hands its descriptor and tag on — no open, no read; anything
else is opened through `openWithinRoot` and hashed. No change → nothing published. A failed rescan
(`TooManyFiles`, I/O) hands every taken-over descriptor back and keeps the current generation.

Publication and reclamation (single publisher, many readers): a request increments
`readers[side]`, reads `side` again (and retries on the other side if it moved), loads `current`, increments that generation's `holds`, decrements
`readers[side]` — and holds the generation for the whole answer. The publisher swaps `current`,
flips `side`, and waits for the old side's readers to drain; after that no request can take the
old generation (a reader that read the old side before the flip was waited for; any later one
loads `current` after the swap). Retired generations are freed only unheld and **oldest first**,
because a descriptor handed on is closed by the generation holding it last — freeing a younger one
before an older one that still serves the same descriptor would close it under that request.
**Bounded retirement** (`LiveOptions.max_retired`, default 16): oldest-first freeing means one slow
download holding generation N pins every later one. At the cap a rescan builds and publishes nothing
(`Outcome.held_back`, `reload` → false): the current generation keeps serving, and the change is
published by the first rescan after the oldest hold is released. Memory and descriptors are bounded
by the module, not by the server's write timeout (nginx and Go serve straight from disk and have no
generations to pin; this is the price of zero syscalls per request, capped).

The re-read of `side` closes a use-after-free: a request that read `side`,
stalled across one whole publish and only then counted itself was counted on the side the NEXT
publisher does not wait for, which freed the generation the request was about to hold (a seam test
reproduces it: segfault without the re-read).

Tested: a held generation keeps serving its bytes across an edit; descriptor counts in
`/proc/self/fd` return exactly to baseline; three reader threads never see anything but one whole
version while the rescan thread swaps.

`LiveOptions.observer` is told each rescan's outcome (`unchanged` / `published` with the
generation and fresh-file count / `failed`) on the thread that ran it — for logs, and for a sandbox
probe that must run code on that thread.

**Replace files atomically** (write + rename). A rename leaves held descriptors on the old inode; a
rewrite in place changes the inode they read, so until the next rescan a request may see it
half-written — inherent to serving from open files, documented, not detected.

## 4. Concurrency & memory

A `Handler` is created once and shared read-only across the server's connection threads; it holds
no mutable state, so `serve` is concurrency-safe. Per-request scratch (ETag, Last-Modified,
Content-Length buffers) is stack-local to the call that computes it, copied by the response
writer's `setHeader` before that call returns — no threadlocal state involved. No dynamic
allocation on the serve path; the 64 KiB streaming buffer is stack-local per request too.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — every path's expected values come from an implementation that is not ours.

**What the tests actually contain.** `src/go_oracle_test.zig` replays Go 1.26 `net/http` answers
(`go_oracle_vectors.zig`, taken by `tools/go_oracle/` over a loopback socket from the very request
bytes the replay sends through `http.Server.serveStream`): 93 path-area cases against
`http.FileServer` (which file, refusal, redirect target — traversal in every encoding, dotfiles,
symlinks in and out of root, trailing slashes, encoded slashes and backslashes, NUL, non-ASCII,
over-long names, methods) and 1282 precondition × range cases against `http.ServeContent` with this
module's own weak and strong size-mtime tags (If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since,
If-Unmodified-Since, If-Range by tag and date, 22 Range shapes, HEAD). 39 path cases and 8 Range
shapes are listed divergences, each judged: Go serves dotfiles, listings, symlinks out of root and
every method, cleans encoded dot-segments, and on Range rejects unknown units and `BYTES`, answers
`bytes=-0` with an invalid `Content-Range`, and does multipart (we serve 200). Before that, and still
present: starlette.staticfiles as a black-box Range/ETag oracle (src/root.zig `interop (starlette
oracle)`). Self only: `Snapshot`/`Live` rescans and content tags, precompressed variant choice, the
MIME table and the listing markup.

Regenerate the Go vectors with `zig build interop-staticfiles` (`-- --check` re-takes and compares);
the producer is `tools/go_oracle/` (`go run . -out ../../src/go_oracle_vectors.zig`).

## Verification

- **Run:** `scripts/modtest staticfiles`; the Go oracle is re-taken by `zig build interop-staticfiles [-- --check]` (needs Go, loopback only).
- **Tests** (`src/root.zig`, `src/go_oracle_test.zig`): the traversal vectors of §1 against a real out-of-root secret and escaping symlinks (including a symlinked directory below depth 1 and a link to the root itself); status mapping, MIME table and overrides, conditional and Range shapes, weak/strong and variant ETags with known answers; precompressed variants and the SPA fallback in `Handler` and `Snapshot`; the listing markup and its limits; `Snapshot` against `Handler` over one fixture tree; `Live` rescans, descriptor counts in `/proc/self/fd` against a baseline, bounded retirement, reader threads against a swapping rescan thread, and seam tests that pause a reader between its steps.
- **Oracles:** Go `net/http` (`go_oracle_vectors.zig`, producer `tools/go_oracle/`) and the starlette black-box transcript, see *Anchoring*.
- **Fuzz:** one harness over `sanitizePath` (accepted paths contain no `..`, NUL, backslash or dotfile unless allowed), run by testkit's deterministic driver as `STATICFILES_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]` (`src/fuzz_test.zig`), with a fixed seed loop and reach checks in every test run.
- **Constant time:** n/a, static file serving.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.
- **Bench:** `zig build bench-staticfiles` (`tools/bench.zig`, with `tools/go_bench` and `tools/rust_fast_bench` as the Go and Rust sides).

## Performance

The bench is `zig build bench-staticfiles` (`BENCH_ROUNDS=5`, ReleaseFast); the card's Performance line carries the figures and is authoritative. A `Handler` request costs one `stat` before the open (it answers a missing name and a directory without the open/fstat/close, and keeps a FIFO from blocking the open); `Snapshot`/`Live` make no filesystem call per request.

## What is deliberately not done

- **A check of `Live`'s descriptors against `RLIMIT_NOFILE`.** Up to `(max_retired + 1) × max_files` descriptors can be open at once (documented on `LiveOptions.max_retired`); neither Go nor nginx checks its descriptor budget against the limit, and the caller who raises `max_files` or `max_retired` owns `ulimit -n`.
- **Multi-range `multipart/byteranges`.** Go and nginx serve it; here a multi-range request answers 200 with the full body, which RFC 7233 §6.1 permits. A known amplification vector; not a backlog item unless a consumer asks.
- **Content sniffing of unknown extensions.** Go sniffs the first 512 bytes; here an unlisted extension is `application/octet-stream` (the embedded table covers the common web types, `Options.mime_overrides` adds more) and `nosniff` tells the browser not to guess.
- **A content-hash `ETag` in `Handler`.** It would turn every conditional GET into a full read; `Snapshot`/`Live` hash once per file at `open`.
- **Staleness and size checks of precompressed siblings.** A `.gz`/`.br`/`.zst` older than its source, or larger than it, is served as is, as nginx `gzip_static` does; the deploy tool owns consistency.
- **`Content-Disposition` or any other way to force a download.** An uploaded `.html`/`.svg` inside the root is served as a document on the serving origin, the same trade-off as Go `FileServer` and nginx.
